title: Why Kabir left Kashi to die
hookLine: a dying poet walks out of the holiest city, on purpose
carry: moksha is god's gift, not a city's
tomorrow: one truth, many names. does that mean all the same?

cards: Many Hindus hope to end their lives in one city: Kashi, also called Benares or Varanasi, on the Ganga. Families still bring their elders there to die. Kabir lived in Kashi nearly all his life.
And at the very end, the story goes, he left. He went to Maghar, a small town with a bad name. A folk saying held that whoever died in Maghar would be born again as a donkey.
His followers begged him to stay. He went anyway. Why?

teach.b: Start with what Kashi means. Hindus call it Shiva's city, and many believe that whoever dies there is freed from the round of birth and death: moksha.

Some say Shiva himself whispers a saving name into the ear of the dying. Most Hindus cremate their dead; the last rite is called antyeshti, the last offering, and many families carry the ashes to the Ganga.
Kabir asked a sharp question about all this.

A line credited to him runs, in paraphrase: if Kabir leaves his body in Kashi, what has Ram done for him? If the city does the freeing, where's God's part? So he went to Maghar to die, trusting Ram's name over the map.
That's a bhakti teaching: moksha is God's gift. When he died, the legend goes, his Hindu followers wanted to cremate him and his Muslim followers wanted to bury him.
They lifted the sheet and found only flowers, and each side took half.

Today at Maghar there are two resting places for him, a samadhi kept in a Hindu way and a mazar, a Muslim tomb, a few steps apart. Two doors, each keeping its own account of his death. And for families now?
Many still hope for the Ganga at the end, and that hope is honored. Kabir only adds: wherever the end comes, God's name reaches there too.

how: Many Hindus hope to die in Kashi (Varanasi), believed to grant moksha, and most Hindus cremate their dead in the rite of antyeshti, often carrying the ashes to the Ganga; at Maghar, where Kabir died, a samadhi and a mazar both honor him.

games.q: what does “never blended as doctrine” mean?
o: shared shrines and songs, each faith keeping its own teaching
the old rule that a saint may be buried in only one way
one new shrine built to replace two older ones nearby

games.q: Kashi and Maghar. tap the pairs.
p: the city where many hope to die

s: a folk saying held that dying in Maghar meant a donkey's rebirth
and Kabir went there anyway, trusting Ram's name.
Kabir taught that the city, not God, does the freeing
the reverse: if Kashi frees you, he asked, what has Ram done?

games.q: your grandfather asked for his ashes to go to the Ganga, but the family can't travel to India this year. a cousin worries he'll miss moksha. what does Kabir's story offer?
o: honor the wish when you can; Kabir taught that moksha is God's gift, not a place's.
there's no hope for him without Kashi or the Ganga.
skip it; rites don't mean anything to Hindus anymore.
games.why: Some families keep the ashes until they can reach the Ganga; others immerse them in a river nearer home. Either way the wish is honored, and Kabir walked to Maghar to say God's name reaches every place.

practice: Kabir walked out of one city and into another. If you can, stand and walk slowly to the nearest doorway. Pause on the threshold and feel the change: the air, the light, the floor under your feet.
Step through and say a name of God once, or, if you don't pray, simply breathe out. Then step back. If standing isn't possible, rest a hand on a door or window frame and feel the line it draws.

wordCard.voice: Never blended as doctrine. At Maghar, a samadhi and a mazar for one man: shared ground, two accounts of his death.

orig.note: Sanskrit: moksha, freedom from the round of birth and death.

carryVoice: Keep this: moksha is God's gift, not a city's. Kabir walked to Maghar to say so. Until tomorrow, then.
